audience: first-year college students, majors and non-majors; advanced layer optional
spine: real gas in space → atoms meet light → the light stretches → motions → velocity space → optical depth → flux → forest → inverse inference

beats.title: Gas occupies real space
beats.statement:
Thin gas fills the space between a distant quasar and us — denser in filaments, emptier in voids.
The quasar's light crosses it along one line. What does the gas along that line do to the light?
beats.objective: There is real gas distributed through a volume, and our light samples one path through it.
beats.action: Move along the beam (hover near it, or press and slide along it); drag the gas to turn the volume. The cross-section, the stretch of the strip and the density reading report where you are.
beats.consequence: The probe follows the hand along the beam; the cut through the volume, the cross-section around the beam, the highlighted stretch of the strip and the density reading follow it. Turned, the volume shows parallax — the beam passes behind near gas and in front of far gas.

equations.note: about a dozen hydrogen nuclei per cubic metre, on average

beats.title: Same gas, different scale
beats.statement:
Zoom into one parcel on the beam: the smooth gas is a crowd of protons, helium nuclei and electrons — atoms with their electrons knocked off by ultraviolet light from galaxies and quasars.
About one hydrogen atom in 100 000 is still neutral (a few times more in a filament) — and only those can absorb the light.
beats.objective: A macroscopic gas parcel is a vast microscopic population, almost all ionised; the atoms drawn next are a representative few.
beats.action: Set the magnification (an instrument setting) from the volume, to one parcel, to its particles, to the neutral atoms.
beats.consequence: Nested frames show the same gas at four scales; the stipple of ionised particles gives way to the rare neutral atoms, which are then gathered for display.

stages.label: volume
stages.text: the gas fills the volume; the beam crosses it

stages.label: particles
stages.text: protons and electrons; a rare neutral atom

equations.note: a 100 kpc (proper) parcel at about 5× the mean density — smaller than the 1 Mpc/h frame drawn; only about one in 10⁵ of these nuclei carries its electron (a neutral atom), the rest are protons and free electrons

simplifications: The observer and the quasar are drawn at the ends of the beam for orientation only; the beam is broken at each end because the gaps are not to scale — the toy sample lies ≈ 4384 Mpc/h (comoving) from us, and the quasar farther still (SCI-RED-004).
The atoms are a representative sample (a few hundred), not a count and not simulation particles (SCI-REP-001).
The particle stage shows the ionised majority as a stipple, with neutral atoms drawn far more common than the true 1 in ~10⁵; from Beat 2 on only neutral atoms are drawn (SCI-ION-002, SCI-REP-006).
Atom motions are straight lines (collisions are rare at these densities) and slowed enormously for display.

beats.title: One atom meets one colour
beats.statement:
Among these colours of the quasar's light, hydrogen responds to one: Lyman-alpha, 1215.67 Å — ultraviolet — in the atom's own frame. (Its weaker siblings, such as Lyman-β, return in Beat 13.)
A moving atom sees colours Doppler-shifted, so a different colour comes into resonance — and is scattered out of the beam.
beats.objective: The physical origin of the shadow is resonant scattering of one colour in the atom's frame.
beats.action: Push the atom along the beam (drag its motion); the speed ruler reports it; switch to "one colour, many atoms".
beats.consequence: A different photon colour is caught and scattered sideways out of the beam; the atom-frame panel shows which colour sits on the resonance.

equations.note: an atom moving away from us (v > 0) brings a redder colour into resonance
the photon is re-emitted, but almost never back into our narrow beam — so it is lost to us

interactions.control: push the atom — grab its motion arrow (or the atom) and drag along the beam (or the left and right arrows); the speed ruler reports it, and the colour that comes into resonance is the one scattered

gesture.mapping: the arrow's tip stays under the hand — {px_per_kms} px per km/s; an arrow key moves it by {key_step_kms} km/s
gesture.metaphor: pushing the atom by hand is a way to explore other speeds along the beam; it does not claim that touching an atom moves it

simplifications: The resonance window is drawn about 500× wider than the true natural width so it is visible (SCI-REP-004).
"Scattered out of the beam" is said here and again in Beat 5, where "shadow" is introduced; elsewhere "removed" or "absorbed" is shorthand (SCI-RES-001).

beats.title: Temperature becomes line width
beats.statement:
A parcel holds many atoms, each moving its own way: temperature is that random motion.
Count them by their speed along the beam: that census is the shape of the line. Hotter gas, wider line — heat sets its core, but not its faint far wings.
beats.objective: Temperature is particle motion, and the thermal line profile is the census of line-of-sight speeds.
beats.action: Hold the gas to explore warmer gas (move down while holding for cooler); the temperature ruler and the reading beside the gas report it; touch the census or the line to see which atoms are there; replay how it forms.
beats.consequence: Atoms move faster and their line-of-sight arrows lengthen; each atom's arrow travels down to a speed ruler (tail at zero) and leaves a mark at its speed; the marks form a band, stack into the census and settle onto its curve; the curve drops into the parcel's line — wider and shallower when hotter, at fixed amount.

stages.label: 3 · the census
stages.text: the marks stack up: how many atoms at each speed

stages.label: 4 · the line
stages.text: the census becomes the parcel’s absorption line

beats.title: The atom's lifetime leaves faint, far wings
beats.statement:
An excited atom does not stay excited forever, so the colour it absorbs is not perfectly sharp.
This lifetime spread is tiny next to the thermal spread — but far from the centre, it wins. In most forest gas these wings are too faint to see; they show only where the beam crosses a very high column of neutral hydrogen (high N_HI).
beats.objective: The Voigt profile has two physically different pieces — a thermal core and lifetime-driven wings.
beats.action: Step through the four statements (a chain of reasoning). With "show the physics", a temperature setting changes the core's width; the wings stay.
beats.consequence: The survival curve decays in ~1.6 ns; the natural line appears as a hairline; inside the thermal core it is invisible; on a logarithmic scale its wings overtake the Gaussian beyond a few b.

stages.label: 2 · so not perfectly sharp

stages.label: 3 · tiny next to motion
stages.text: thermal motion is well over a thousand times wider

stages.label: 4 · far out, it wins
stages.text: the wings reach farther than the Gaussian

x = Δv/b; core + wings — the full Voigt function is in the microscope

micro.ask: why does a short life spread the colour?

simplifications: The surface shows only the survival probability; the classical damped-oscillator analogue is in the microscope, labelled as an analogue (SCI-NAT-001).
The natural line is magnified (×1200) in the inset and labelled (SCI-REP-004).

beats.title: The same colour, stretched
beats.statement:
Hydrogen absorbs at Lyman-alpha in its own frame, scattering that colour out of the beam: a shadow.
Between the gas and us the universe expands: the light stretches, and every shadow written in it stretches too.
beats.objective: Lyα absorption is local and always at 1215.67 Å in the absorber's own frame; the forest is many such shadows, written at different redshifts and stretched on to us, so observed wavelength records where along the way each was written.
beats.action: Drag the light along its path (or step through, or play, the journey); select a structure in the gas; at the end, zoom into one shadow.
beats.consequence: The whole spectral ribbon stretches past a fixed Lyα mark; each structure writes a shadow where the ribbon sits under the mark; earlier shadows move redward as the stretching continues, behind the quasar's own Lyα, which rides the ribbon as a quiet anchor ahead of them all (the close-up keeps a trail of its drift); at our telescope the shadows form the observed forest, the selected one at 1215.67 × (1 + z) Å.

stages.text: at 1215.67 Å in its own frame

stages.label: 3 · it stretches on
stages.text: the shadow moves redward with the light

stages.label: 4 · the next structure
stages.text: writes at its own Lyα, on a different part of the light

in the quasar's rest frame every intervening shadow lies blueward of the quasar's own Lyα

beats.title: Where does one parcel land?
beats.statement:
One parcel of gas from the 4.4 Mpc/h stretch around the selected shadow. Move it, push it, warm it, or change how much of it is neutral.
Each changes one thing about its ink — its contribution to optical depth — on the spectrum: where it lands (where its ink appears in the spectrum, not where the gas is), how wide, or how much.
beats.objective: Position and bulk velocity set where the contribution lands; temperature and the parcel's size (the Hubble flow across it) set its spread; the neutral amount sets how much — ink is its contribution to optical depth τ.
beats.action: Move the gas along the beam (its place); push its motion; hold it to explore warmer gas; set the amount of neutral hydrogen with the margin instrument. The rulers and the readings beside the gas report each change; a pencil ghost keeps the state before.
beats.consequence: Moving it farther lengthens its recession from the expansion, so it lands redder; pushing it moves where it lands without moving it in space; warmer gas spreads the same ink wider; more neutral hydrogen deepens the ink in place. The ledger place · motion · width · amount marks what changed and what did not; the comparison with the ghost is measured.

equations.note: place

equations.tex: b^2 \simeq \dfrac{2kT}{m_{\rm H}} + b_{\rm size}^2,\qquad b_{\rm size} = \sqrt{2}\,aH\,\sigma_x
equations.note: spread: heat and the parcel's size (the Hubble flow across its width σ_x) add in quadrature; here b_size = 23.8 km/s, comparable to the thermal 21.4 km/s
amount and spread, with the b above (the drawn line's); σ_v = (πe²/m_e c) f λ₀

beats.title: Distance and observed colour are not the same coordinate
beats.statement:
Now the parcel's neighbours: three parcels from the same stretch. Under expansion alone, farther gas recedes faster, so they land in order.
Now push one along the line of sight: its threads (from the gas to where it lands) tilt, and the gas can land out of order — and the gas between the parcels lands too.
beats.objective: The spectrum is organised in observed velocity (wavelength), not simply by real-space distance.
beats.action: Push a parcel (grab its velocity arrow) and drag its line-of-sight velocity; touch a parcel's gas to select it; switch between expansion alone and the toy's velocities; touch velocity space to see which gas lands there.
beats.consequence: Each parcel hangs fine threads from where its gas is to where it lands; they hang straight under pure expansion, tilt with peculiar velocity, fold where the gas converges in velocity, and cross when the order reverses; the flux forms where they land; pencil ghosts mark where expansion alone would put each parcel.

equations.note: x_com comoving; v_pec > 0 means moving away from us (redder); here aH(z)/h = 114.2 km s⁻¹ per Mpc/h (Planck 2018, z = 3)
the ruler converts velocity to observed wavelength (the stretch of Beat 5, measured in km/s)

beats.title: From parcels back to a continuous sightline
beats.statement:
The three parcels were a teaching summary. Cut the same stretch finer — tens of cells, then the full sampling.
Every cell follows the same rule: map, place its optical depth (its ink), broaden — and the contributions combine.
beats.objective: The toy rules apply cell by cell to a continuous, finely sampled sightline.
beats.action: Drag the number of cells from 3 up to the full sampling.
beats.consequence: The strip goes from three smudges to ruled cells to a continuous band; the optical depth converges to the full calculation (dashed).

equations.note: the continuous version of "every cell contributes"

valid where each sampling element has one velocity and lines span at least two pixels; outside that domain, particle-based codes differ (up to 0.2 in F for unresolved velocity structure, up to 0.46 for lines narrower than two pixels) — stated, not hidden

simplifications: Real-space cells are the gas re-sampled on a line; particle codes such as fake_spectra deposit each particle's kernel directly in velocity space (VAL-CLOSURE-FS, SCI-SIM-002).

One velocity and one temperature per cell. Where several velocities share one cell (unresolved velocity structure), absorption is misplaced; the toy stores one mass-weighted velocity per cell — it discards sub-cell velocity structure by design (SCI-TAU-004).
The sum converges only once cells are finer than the narrowest line (aH·Δx ≤ b/2); the coarse slider settings are deliberately under-resolved (SCI-TAU-005).

beats.title: Ink adds
beats.statement:
Every cell has laid its ink in velocity space. Where contributions overlap, they stack.
The ink is optical depth — optical depths add. Dips in the light, the shadows, do not.
beats.objective: Optical depth is the additive quantity.
beats.action: Play the stacking; toggle "what if dips added instead?".
beats.consequence: Transparent contributions stack into the total τ; the wrong rule (adding flux decrements) produces impossible negative light.

equations.note: absorbers act independently; their optical depths add

simplifications: The stretch is drawn as 24 cells, coarser than Beat 8's criterion for convergence (half the narrowest line's width); the footer states how far their transmitted flux then differs from the full sampling (SCI-TAU-005).
Each cell's optical depth is drawn as one transparent layer of ink; the layers picture the sum, not a physical order along the beam (SCI-REP-005).

beats.title: Light multiplies
beats.statement:
Put the inked ribbon on a light table. Each layer passes a fraction of the light; the fractions multiply.
Where the ink is thick almost nothing gets through: the line saturates, and stops getting deeper. The backlit ribbon is the spectrum of this stretch.
beats.objective: Transmitted flux is F = e^−τ, so transmissions multiply where optical depths add.
beats.action: Drag the loupe along the ribbon (or along the spectrum) to hold any colour to the light; open "why does a line stop getting deeper?".
beats.consequence: The backlit ribbon glows warm where light gets through and stays dark where it does not; the light it lets through also lights the paper around it; the probe lists each layer's transmission and their product; the flux curve is drawn from the light that gets through.

equations.note: the ribbon is rendered by stacking layers of opacity 1 − e^−τᵢ — the picture performs the rule

interactions.control: move the loupe along the ribbon or along the spectrum — by hovering, dragging or touch

gesture.mapping: the loupe's colour is the colour under the hand, on the ribbon or on the spectrum below it; moving it {learned_px} px counts as discovered

interactions.variable: the colour held to the light, u [km/s] (the window's range)

visual_transforms.from: each cell's optical depth τᵢ at each colour
visual_transforms.to: transmitted light e^(−Στᵢ) = Πe^(−τᵢ) (layers of opacity 1 − e^(−τᵢ) over a warm backlight)

micro.ask: why does a line stop getting deeper?

simplifications: The quasar's intrinsic spectrum (continuum) is divided out; F = 1 means "all the expected light arrived".

beats.title: A forest emerges
beats.statement:
Run the same rules along the toy's full 20 Mpc/h, not just 4.4: the Lyman-alpha forest up close, from 4 863 Å. Dense filaments write its deep lines.
A spectrograph blurs and adds noise to what we record — the gas and its optical depth are untouched.
beats.objective: The forest is the same rules at scale; instrument resolution and noise act only on the final observation.
beats.action: Zoom out; set the spectrograph's resolution and signal-to-noise (instrument settings — the gas does not change, the measurement does).
beats.consequence: The recorded spectrum smooths and gets noisy; the gas strip and τ are visibly unchanged.

equations.note: resolution convolves the transmitted flux, not the optical depth
white noise per detector pixel
the observed-wavelength ruler — Beat 5's stretch, read in km/s
broken line: the data producer's own spectrum (exact Voigt, an independent code path); the browser's differs by at most 6e-04 in F

simplifications: The observer and the quasar are drawn at the ends of the beam for orientation only; the beam is broken at each end because the gaps are not to scale — the toy sample lies ≈ 4384 Mpc/h (comoving) from us, and the quasar farther still (SCI-RED-004).

The toy sightline's τ normalisation (Γ_HI) is tuned so the mean transmitted flux is 0.68, as measured at z ≈ 3; the tuned Γ_HI (2.4×10⁻¹² s⁻¹) is ~3× the measured 0.8×10⁻¹², so the toy's absolute ionisation is not a physical claim (SCI-SIM-TOY-001, SCI-CTX-003, SCI-CTX-004).
Gaussian line-spread function and white noise of constant σ (SCI-OBS-001, SCI-OBS-002).
The student-facing spectrum is the app's own; the generating code's spectrum, an independent check, is an overlay in "show the physics".

beats.title: Who ate this colour?
beats.statement:
The recorded spectrum is all an observer gets. Go backwards — here we can, because we built the gas: point at a colour and light up the gas that absorbed it.
Sometimes one region dominates; sometimes separate places share one colour.
beats.objective: One spectral pixel is not automatically one place in the gas; optical depths from many places add.
beats.action: Press the spectrum and slide along it — the first time, the colour is traced back slowly; then every colour answers at once (or use the arrow keys); touch the gas to see which colours it takes.
beats.consequence: A cinnabar thread rises from the colour into the optical depth, splits by contribution and lands on the gas that absorbed it; those regions develop like ink; then their shares appear and a ledger writes out τ as a sum and F as a product, and the threads fade.

equations.note: a colour's optical depth is a sum over all the gas that lands there; the light that gets through is the product

interactions.control: press the spectrum and slide along it (or the arrow keys); the causal cursor follows the finger; the wavelength ruler is a reading, not a handle

gesture.mapping: the colour examined is the colour under the finger on the spectrum or its optical-depth band

simplifications: The observer and the quasar are drawn at the ends of the beam for orientation only; the beam is broken at each end because the gaps are not to scale — the toy sample lies ≈ 4384 Mpc/h (comoving) from us, and the quasar farther still (SCI-RED-004).
Shares are computed from the same browser model as the spectrum; regions are grouped by contiguity along the line (the grouping is a display choice).

beats.title: Same shadow
beats.statement:
Now only the recorded line, as an observer has it — no gas to look up. Three different gases could have made it.
Predict which — then see why the shadow alone cannot tell, and what can.
beats.objective: The spectrum carries physical information, but the inverse problem is not unique; inference must be calibrated, not abandoned.
beats.action: Choose a gas; reveal; then add a heavier-ion line or Lyman-beta.
beats.consequence: All three gases fit the observed line, for two different reasons — the blend (ii) only because of the noise, (iii) because heat and smooth motion widen every hydrogen line alike; a metal line separates heat from bulk motion, and Lyman-beta exposes the hidden column of the blend.

equations.note: heat broadens light atoms more than heavy ions; bulk motion broadens all alike — every hydrogen line (Lyα, Lyβ, …) sees only the total b, so heat and smooth motion can match in all of them
the blend (ii) is hidden by the noise: at S/N = 50 it shows (Δχ² ≈ 17). (iii) is hidden by what hydrogen records; its small misfit is the hand-tuning, not physics
inside the saturated Lyα core almost no light gets through, however the optical depth is split — so the blend (ii) hides there; Lyβ, with a smaller f λ, is not saturated and shows it

simplifications: The three configurations were tuned by hand to match. Two kinds of "same shadow" are shown — the blend (ii) is hidden only at the stated resolution and S/N (measurement-limited: better data can break it); heat against smooth motion, (i) against (iii), cannot be told apart by any hydrogen line at any S/N (information-limited: hydrogen records only the line-of-sight distribution of velocity and optical depth). The toy's small misfit for (iii) is its hand-tuning (SCI-DEG-001).
The three gases are called "clouds" for brevity; each is a denser part of the continuous gas, idealised as one or two smooth Gaussian clumps — not a separate object (SCI-REP-003).

The three configurations are a constructed degeneracy example, not typical forest absorbers. Configuration (i) is an idealised compact gas clump — unusually hot (45 000 K, hotter than typical forest gas at z ≈ 3) and only about 7 kpc across (proper), far more compact than typical forest gas — built so that its line matches the other two (SCI-DEG-001).
